title: Lehmann’s inner core
teaches: Faint waves inside the shadow zone, the solid inner core they revealed, and how its growth powers the magnetic field

blocks.text: Inge Lehmann trained as a mathematician in Copenhagen and in 1928 became head of the seismology department of Denmark's new Geodetic Institute, responsible for the country's seismograph stations in Denmark and Greenland. Much of her work was the routine of reading records and measuring arrival times. She kept her notes on cardboard cards, sorted in oat boxes.

blocks.caption: Inge Lehmann (1888–1993), who discovered the Earth's inner core.

blocks.text: On 17 June 1929 a magnitude 7.3 earthquake struck near Murchison, in the northern South Island of New Zealand. New Zealand is almost directly opposite Europe on the globe, so European stations lie between about 140° and 180° away, the zone where waves have crossed the core (lesson D4). Studying those records, and others like them, Lehmann noticed something that the standard picture did not allow. Faint P waves were arriving at distances inside the shadow zone, from about 105° to 140°, where no direct wave was supposed to land.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Lehmann ran Denmark's seismograph stations from 1928.
In records of the 1929 Murchison earthquake in New Zealand, she found faint P waves arriving inside the shadow zone.

blocks.text: Lehmann proposed a simple explanation in 1936, in a paper titled only "P′" (P-prime, the seismologists' label for P waves that cross the core). Suppose the core has an inner part where waves travel faster than in the outer core. A wave that crosses the outer core steeply enough to reach this inner core speeds up there and is bent outward, away from the centre, the opposite of what happens at the outer core's edge. Some waves are bent enough to come back out and land inside the shadow. They are faint, because only a narrow range of paths does this, and much of the energy is reflected or spread thin.

blocks.caption: The Earth from lesson D4, with the liquid outer core in place. Add an inner core where P waves travel at about 11 km/s; rose paths are those that enter it.
blocks.task: Add an inner core big enough to send waves into the shadow

blocks.text: Her model was rough: a single shell with constant speeds. But within a few years Beno Gutenberg and Charles Richter, and Harold Jeffreys, had confirmed the inner core with more records. Lehmann had put its edge at about 5,000 kilometres down; the modern figure is 5,150, which gives the inner core a radius of 1,220 kilometres, about two-thirds the size of the Moon.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Lehmann (1936) proposed an inner core where waves travel faster, bending some of them outward into the shadow zone.
The inner core's edge is 5,150 km down; it has a radius of 1,220 km.

blocks.text: Why should the innermost core be different? The obvious idea was that it is solid while the outer core is liquid, but proving it took until 1971. Very large earthquakes set the whole Earth ringing like a bell for days, at a set of exact frequencies that depend on the stiffness of every layer. Adam Dziewonski and Freeman Gilbert analysed the ringing after the great earthquakes of the 1960s and showed that the inner core must be rigid: it is solid iron and nickel.

The temperature at the centre is over 5,000 °C, hotter than the outer core. The inner core is solid anyway because of pressure. The pressure there is more than three million times that at the surface, and pressure makes it harder for atoms to break free of the ordered arrangement of a solid, which raises the melting point. Going down through the core, the melting point rises faster than the temperature does. At 5,150 kilometres down the two cross, and below that depth the iron freezes.

blocks.caption: An iron meteorite, etched to show its crystals. The inner core is thought to be a solid alloy of iron and nickel, much like this.

blocks.text: As the Earth slowly loses heat, more of the outer core freezes onto the inner core, which grows by perhaps a millimetre a year. Freezing releases heat and leaves the remaining liquid richer in lighter elements such as oxygen and sulphur, which rise. Both stir the outer core and help keep the molten iron churning, and that churning drives the magnetic field of lesson 9. The inner core may be younger than the Earth itself, perhaps only one or two billion years old, though the age is debated.
Lehmann worked on the Earth's interior for the rest of her long life. She continued to publish into her nineties, and died in 1993 at 104.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Dziewonski and Gilbert (1971) showed from the Earth's ringing after great earthquakes that the inner core is solid.
Pressure raises the melting point of iron faster than the temperature rises with depth, so the centre is solid though hotter than the outer core.
The inner core grows as the outer core freezes onto it, which helps power the magnetic field.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the inner core
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why were the faint waves Lehmann saw surprising?
choices: They arrived inside the shadow zone, where no direct P wave was supposed to land
They arrived before the earthquake happened
They were S waves that had crossed the liquid core
items.why: The core's shadow was expected to be empty of direct P waves between about 104° and 140°.

items.ask: How does an inner core send waves into the shadow?
choices: Waves speed up in it and are bent outward, so some emerge at distances inside the shadow
It reflects all waves straight back to the quake
It slows waves until they stop
items.why: Entering faster material bends a wave away from the steeper direction, the opposite of what the slower outer core does.

items.ask: Why is the inner core solid when it is hotter than the liquid outer core?
choices: The pressure there raises iron's melting point above the temperature
It is made of rock, not iron
It is cooled by the outer core
items.why: With depth the melting point rises faster than the temperature. Below 5,150 km, the melting point wins.

items.ask: How was the inner core shown to be solid in 1971?
choices: From the frequencies at which the whole Earth rings after great earthquakes
From the colour of volcanic lava
items.why: The Earth's ringing depends on the stiffness of every layer. Dziewonski and Gilbert found the inner core must be rigid.

items.ask: How does the growing inner core help the magnetic field?
choices: Freezing releases heat and light elements that stir the liquid outer core, which generates the field
The solid inner core is a permanent magnet
It blocks the Sun's magnetic field
items.why: The field comes from moving, conducting liquid iron. Freezing at the inner core's surface helps keep it moving.

learned: Lehmann (1936) explained faint P waves in the shadow zone with a faster inner core.
The inner core, 1,220 km in radius, is solid iron and nickel, shown in 1971 from the Earth's ringing.
Pressure keeps the centre solid though it is over 5,000 °C, and the freezing inner core helps power the magnetic field.
